A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SCT-based automatic sparse differentiation work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching Hessian material moved into v2's appendices.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendices A.8–A.9 report original timing experiments for sparsity detection and Jacobian/Hessian computation on the Brusselator and PGLib problems.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical benchmarks and adds runtime decomposition, Newton-step solver timings, and implicit-GNN training and test results in Section 5 and Appendix G.

M1.justification: The operator-overloaded tracers, local/global classifications, tensor overloads, and detection–coloring–differentiation pipeline are retained. Configurable sparsity representations already appeared in v1 Appendix A.5. v2 expands implementation documentation and applies the approach to additional evaluations without establishing a changed SCT algorithm.

E1.justification: v2 adds node classification using an implicit GNN on simplified synthetic chains (Section 5.2), and extends Brusselator evaluation to Newton linear-system solves (Appendix G.2). These introduce downstream tasks beyond derivative construction. The original Brusselator, PGLib, and convolutional examples remain.

E2.justification: The original Symbolics/SCT and dense-AD/ASD comparisons remain. v2 additionally evaluates VJP-based GMRES against sparse direct solves for GNN differentiation, and lazy-JVP and materialized-Jacobian BiCGStab(l) against direct Newton solves. These substantially expand the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: The new GNN protocol uses 10-node chains, 100 input features, 16 hidden units, and one positive and one negative training chain, reporting loss and test accuracy against time. Its iterative and direct arms use Zygote and ForwardDiff respectively. Newton-step timing also introduces a new protocol; the original benchmark grid, hardware, and derivative backends remain.

E4.justification: v2 Figure 2 adds an explicit runtime-component breakdown examining the sparsity-detection bottleneck. Figure 5b adds a local sparsity example alongside the retained global convolution patterns. These are limited diagnostic additions beyond v1's aggregate timing comparisons and global-pattern illustrations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars. Parenthetical timing-table values remain speedup ratios, and the new GNN curves show epochs without uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Brusselator timings are revised: at N=192, unprepared ASD changes from 10.4 seconds in v1 Table 6 to 4.62 seconds in v2 Table 4 under the same stated grid and backend. v2 adds solver timings, runtime components, and GNN curves reporting nearly twofold faster epochs. All 41 PGLib rows in each full results table are unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 replaces gradient and Hessian sparsity equalities with upper bounds, adds a cancellation counterexample, and restores the missing minus sign in the implicit derivative formula. Appendix C adds formal compression/coloring conditions, although its greedy star-coloring wording conflicts with its own definition. The original tracing derivations otherwise remain.

C1.justification: v1 presents a novel three-package ASD pipeline as a principal contribution; v2 makes SCT sparsity detection the primary contribution and treats coloring and differentiation packages as supporting infrastructure. This substantially narrows the contribution framing and adds GNNs to the claimed application scope, while retaining the one-off computation and large-speedup claims.

C2.justification: v2 expands brief control-flow/GPU caveats into specific unsupported operations, explanations of unsafe sparsity underestimation, and memory-allocation and block-sparsity limitations. New solver discussions explain conditioning, precision, and JVP-count tradeoffs. The GNN discussion also acknowledges that different AD backends may partly explain its speedup.

D1.justification: v2 documents overload code generation and correctness checks, extension hooks, alternative sparsity representations, and coloring/decompression details. It supplies new GNN and solver configurations and replaces the anonymous repository reference with a named repository and archived release citation. These substantially expand documentation without establishing changes to the original implementation.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of Lohoff and Neftci's Graphax approach, implicit-GNN literature, and additional coloring and solver references. Separate companion papers now document the differentiation interface and coloring package. Some citations, including AbstractDifferentiation, disappear, but the historical account and operator-overloading lineage remain largely intact.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contributions, and software narrative are extensively refocused around SCT. Applications move into the introduction; Hessian theory and experiments move into appendices; implementation material becomes organized subsections on representations, tensor overloads, and limitations. This is substantial restructuring beyond simply adding experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds runtime-breakdown and GNN-training figures, expands the convolution figure with a local-pattern panel, and restructures the Brusselator table with Newton-solver columns. Duplicate main-text Brusselator-pattern and selected PGLib displays disappear while their appendix content remains. Captions and code-listing presentation are also revised.

improvement.justification: v1's efficiency evidence centers on derivative construction. v2 addresses the important downstream-use gap through Newton and GNN solver comparisons, adds bottleneck diagnostics, corrects central mathematical statements, and documents concrete failure conditions while preserving the Hessian evidence. These substantially strengthen usefulness and credibility. The toy GNN's different AD backends limit causal attribution, and the new coloring primer contains a local inconsistency, but these limitations do not outweigh the gains.
